los.text: Perform a structured examination of the eyes, assessing external and internal features.
los.html:
StepDetail
InspectEyelids (ptosis, lesions), conjunctiva (redness, pallor), sclera (jaundice), cornea (clarity, ulcers), pupils (size, shape, symmetry), exophthalmos
Visual acuityEach eye separately with glasses/pinhole (Snellen)
Visual fieldsConfrontation
PupilsDirect, consensual, swinging light test (RAPD), accommodation
Eye movementsH pattern
FundoscopyRed reflex, optic disc, vessels, retina, macula

los.text: Use an ophthalmoscope to examine the fundus of the eye.
los.html:
1Dim the room; ask the patient to look at a distant fixed point.
2
  • Set the lens to 0 (or your correction)
  • Right hand, right eye to examine the patient's right eye (and left for left).
3From ~30 cm, check the red reflex (absent: cataract, retinoblastoma in children).
4
  • Move in at ~15° from the side
  • Focus on the optic disc: colour (pale = atrophy)
  • Cup-to-disc ratio (large = glaucoma)
  • Margins (blurred and swollen = papilloedema).
5Follow the vessels out in four directions (AV nipping, haemorrhages), then look at the macula (ask to look into the light) last.
FindingSuggests
Swollen disc, blurred marginsPapilloedema (raised ICP)
Dot/blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms, exudates, new vesselsDiabetic retinopathy
AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spotsHypertensive retinopathy
Cherry-red spot, pale retinaCentral retinal artery occlusion
"Stormy sunset" haemorrhagesCentral retinal vein occlusion

los.text: Describe how the extraocular muscles control eye movement and pupil response.
los.html:
MuscleActionNerve
Lateral rectusAbductionVI
Medial rectusAdductionIII
Superior rectusElevation (best when abducted)III
Inferior rectusDepression (best when abducted)III
Superior obliqueDepression when adducted (intorsion)IV
Inferior obliqueElevation when adductedIII
Levator palpebraeLifts the lidIII (+ sympathetic)
  • "LR6 SO4, rest 3".
  • Pupil response: light
    • → optic nerve (afferent)
    • → pretectal nuclei
    • → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei
    • → oculomotor nerve (efferent, parasympathetic)
    • → ciliary ganglion
    • → constriction of both pupils (direct and consensual).
    • Dilation: sympathetic.

los.text: Test peripheral vision and visual acuity using standard clinical techniques.
los.html:
TestHow
Visual acuity
  • Snellen chart at 6 m, each eye separately with glasses
  • Record as 6/6 (distance/line read)
  • Pinhole improves refractive error
  • Near vision chart
Visual fields (confrontation)
  • Sit 1 m away at eye level
  • Patient covers one eye, looks at your opposite eye
  • Bring a red hat pin or wiggling finger in from the periphery in each quadrant
  • Compare with your own fields
InattentionBoth hands at once
Blind spotRed pin
Field defectLesion
One eye blindOptic nerve
Bitemporal hemianopiaOptic chiasm (pituitary)
Homonymous hemianopiaOptic tract/radiation/occipital cortex (stroke)
Superior quadrantanopiaTemporal lobe

los.text: Take a focused history from a patient presenting with an ophthalmological symptom and explain the diagnosis clearly using patient-friendly language, demonstrating effective communication
los.html:
Eye history
Symptom: red eye (pain? discharge? photophobia?), vision loss (sudden/gradual, one/both eyes, painful/painless), floaters and flashes, double vision
  • Red flags: sudden vision loss
  • Painful red eye with reduced vision (acute glaucoma, keratitis, uveitis)
  • New floaters/flashes with a curtain (retinal detachment)
  • Headache with jaw claudication (giant cell arteritis)
Background: glasses/contacts, diabetes, hypertension, eye drops, family history (glaucoma), trauma
  • Explaining (e.g. bacterial conjunctivitis or cataract): plain words
    • what it is
    • treatment
    • what to expect
    • when to seek help (worse pain, vision changes)
    • check understanding.
